questions.text: Stemming vs lemmatization in 30 seconds — and name a production case where each is the right call.
points: Stemming: rule-based suffix chopping (Porter-style) — fast, no dictionary, output often isn't a word ("studies"→"studi"). Lemmatization: vocabulary + morphology (needs POS) mapping to the dictionary lemma ("better"→"good") — slower, linguistically correct.
Both exist to collapse inflectional variants so "run/runs/running" match — a recall device for sparse-feature systems.

Stemming's home: search indexing at scale — recall matters, users never see the stems, throughput is high. Lemmatization's home: anywhere output or features are human-visible or semantically sensitive (linguistic features, aspect extraction).

The modern caveat that scores points: subword tokenization and contextual models made both largely obsolete in the neural path — you normalize much less aggressively for transformer inputs, because the model handles morphology; over-normalization now destroys signal (negations, case, morphology).
So the honest 2026 answer: they survive in the sparse/BM25 side of hybrid stacks and in low-resource/cheap pipelines — know them as index-time analyzers, not as default preprocessing.
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: Stemming chops fast for search indexes where recall wins, lemmatization maps to real lemmas where humans see the output — and in the neural path both mostly retired, because subwords and context handle morphology better than destructive normalization.

questions.text: BPE, WordPiece, Unigram — how do subword tokenizers differ, and why did subwords win over words and characters?
points: Why subwords won: word vocabularies can't cover open vocabulary (OOV → UNK destroys information; vocabulary explodes across morphology); characters cover everything but produce long sequences with weak units. Subwords interpolate: common words stay whole, rare words decompose into meaningful pieces — no UNK, bounded vocab, tractable lengths.
BPE: start from characters, greedily merge the most frequent pair repeatedly until vocab size — simple, deterministic; byte-level BPE guarantees coverage of any string.
WordPiece: merges chosen by likelihood gain on a language model objective rather than raw frequency (BERT-family).

Unigram: start big, prune tokens to maximize corpus likelihood under a unigram model — probabilistic, supports sampling multiple segmentations (subword regularization) as augmentation. SentencePiece packages Unigram/BPE language-agnostically (no pre-tokenization by spaces — matters for Japanese/Chinese/Thai).

Production consequences to voice: vocabulary is frozen with the model (domain drift → fragmenting of your key terms → more tokens, worse cost/quality), and tokenizer mismatch between components (embedder vs generator) is a real integration bug class.
questions.badge: Trending — subword mechanics recur on LeetCode Discuss + every LLM-adjacent screen (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Subwords beat words on OOV and characters on sequence length — BPE merges by frequency, WordPiece by likelihood gain, Unigram prunes a big vocab probabilistically — and since the vocab freezes with the model, domain-term fragmentation becomes a cost and quality tax you should check on your own corpus.

questions.text: Your team preprocesses text with lowercase + stopword removal + stemming before feeding a transformer. Review that pipeline.
points: The pipeline is cargo-culted from the sparse era — those steps fought BoW/TF-IDF sparsity by collapsing variants. Transformers were pretrained on raw-ish text: matching the pretraining distribution matters more than shrinking the feature space.

What each step destroys: lowercasing kills case signal (NER, acronyms, "US" vs "us") if the model is cased; stopword removal deletes exactly the function words transformers use for syntax and negation ("not good" → "good" is a sentiment-flipping bug); stemming feeds the tokenizer malformed strings it fragments into junk subwords.

The correct transformer-side preprocessing is minimal: Unicode normalization, whitespace cleanup, handling encoding junk, maybe URL/emoji policy decisions — then let the model's own tokenizer do its job.

The nuance that shows seniority: the sparse arm of a hybrid system (BM25 index) still legitimately uses aggressive analyzers — different representation, different rules; the bug is applying one arm's preprocessing to the other.
Verify empirically: A/B the pipeline on your eval set — over-preprocessing usually costs measurable accuracy, and that number ends the debate faster than doctrine.
questions.badge: Trending — the "legacy preprocessing habits" trap recurs on interview roundups (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: That's sparse-era preprocessing applied to a model pretrained on raw text — lowercasing kills case signal, stopword removal deletes negation, stemming feeds the tokenizer junk — so keep transformer input minimal and save the aggressive analyzers for the BM25 arm where they belong.

questions.text: TF-IDF: derive the intuition for both terms, and tell me why it's still in production everywhere in 2026.
points: TF: a term matters more in a document the more it appears there (usually dampened — log/sublinear — because the 10th occurrence adds less than the 1st). IDF: a term matters less globally the more documents contain it — log(N/df) → stopwords score ~0, rare discriminative terms score high. The product weights "characteristic of this document".

Why it survives: near-zero cost at enormous scale, fully interpretable (you can read why a document matched), no training required, and it handles exact/rare tokens — IDs, SKUs, error codes, names — that dense embeddings blur. Plus it's the feature layer for logistic-regression baselines that still win on cost for many classification tasks.

Its blind spots define its complement: no synonymy ("car" ≠ "automobile"), no word order, no context — exactly what dense vectors provide, which is why hybrid sparse+dense is the modern equilibrium rather than either alone.
Know the lineage: TF-IDF's probabilistic descendant is BM25 (saturation + length normalization) — in interviews, moving fluidly from TF-IDF to BM25 is expected.
Related classics one sentence deep: PMI/PPMI (association strength between words), LSA (SVD over the term-doc matrix — the ancestor of embeddings).
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: TF says important-in-this-document, IDF says informative-across-the-corpus — and it survives because it's free, interpretable, and exact-match-faithful on the rare tokens embeddings blur, which is precisely the half of hybrid retrieval that dense vectors can't do.

questions.text: Cosine vs Jaccard vs Euclidean for text similarity — when does the choice actually change the answer?
points: Cosine compares direction, ignoring vector length — the default for TF-IDF and embeddings because document length shouldn't dominate similarity; a tweet and an essay about the same topic can still align.

Euclidean mixes direction with magnitude — on unnormalized counts, long documents drift far from everything; note the equivalence worth saying: on L2-normalized vectors, cosine and Euclidean give identical rankings, so the fight only matters unnormalized.

Jaccard operates on sets (overlap/union of tokens or shingles) — no weights, no geometry; the right tool for near-duplicate detection and short-text overlap, and it's what MinHash approximates at scale for dedup.

Where the choice bites in production: ANN indexes are built for a specific metric (cosine/inner-product/L2) — index metric must match the embedding model's training metric or rankings quietly degrade; and inner product ≠ cosine when vectors aren't normalized (recommendation embeddings often exploit magnitude deliberately).
The interview move: state that for embeddings the model's training objective decides the metric — you don't choose it aesthetically.

questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: Cosine compares direction and forgives length, Euclidean punishes magnitude unless you've normalized — at which point they rank identically — and Jaccard is set overlap for dedup; in production the embedding model's training metric decides, and the ANN index must match it.

questions.text: Word2Vec: skip-gram, negative sampling, and why any of this still matters in the contextual-embedding era.
points: The premise: the distributional hypothesis — words in similar contexts mean similar things — operationalized as a prediction task. Skip-gram: predict context words from the center word (better for rare words); CBOW: predict center from averaged context (faster).

Negative sampling is the scalability trick: full softmax over the vocabulary is intractable, so replace it with binary classification — real (word, context) pairs vs k sampled fake ones — turning each update into k+1 logistic regressions. This trick (contrastive learning against negatives) is the direct ancestor of modern embedding-model training — that lineage is the answer's payoff.

GloVe gets similar vectors from global co-occurrence-matrix factorization; fastText adds character n-grams — subword composition gives vectors for unseen/misspelled words, still uniquely handy for noisy text.
The structural limit that ended the era: one vector per type — "bank" has a single point regardless of sentence; contextual models (ELMo onward) give tokens context-dependent vectors.

Why it still matters practically: static embeddings remain unbeatable on cost for lightweight similarity, cold-start features, and edge deployment — and the negative-sampling/contrastive framing is the conceptual key to everything from sentence embeddings to retrieval bi-encoders.
questions.badge: Evergreen — still the canonical "do you understand embeddings" question.
questions.oneLiner: Word2Vec turns the distributional hypothesis into predict-your-context, made tractable by negative sampling — contrastive learning that today's embedding models still descend from — with its one-vector-per-word limit being exactly what contextual models fixed.

questions.text: Sentence embeddings: why does averaging BERT token vectors give bad similarity, and what fixed it?
points: The failure: vanilla BERT token-averaging (or [CLS]) produces vectors that cluster by surface artifacts — the space is anisotropic and was never optimized so that similar meaning → nearby points; cosine over raw BERT often loses to TF-IDF.

The fix (Sentence-BERT lineage): contrastive fine-tuning — siamese/bi-encoder training on pairs (paraphrases, question-answer, positives + hard negatives) that explicitly pulls related sentences together and pushes unrelated apart. The objective, not the architecture, creates the similarity geometry.
Hard negatives are the secret ingredient: training against near-misses (same topic, wrong answer) is what makes retrieval embeddings sharp; random negatives are too easy and produce mushy spaces.

Consequence for practitioners: pick embedding models by retrieval benchmarks and your own eval, not by base-model prestige; and note the task-prefix era (models trained with "query:" / "passage:" asymmetry) — using them without the prefixes silently degrades.
Evaluation habit: intrinsic scores (STS correlations) are hints; your corpus's recall@k is the decision metric — embedding leaderboards suffer the same contamination/mismatch caveats as LLM ones.
questions.badge: Trending — the bi-encoder training story recurs in retrieval-heavy screens (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Raw BERT averaging fails because nothing in pretraining made sentence vectors comparable — contrastive bi-encoder fine-tuning with hard negatives builds the similarity geometry, which is why embedding models are chosen by retrieval evals and used with the exact query-passage conventions they were trained on.

questions.text: N-gram language models and smoothing: what problem does smoothing solve, and what's the one smoothing idea worth remembering?
points: N-gram LMs estimate P(word | previous n−1 words) from counts under a Markov assumption. The fatal flaw: any unseen n-gram gets probability zero, and one zero annihilates the whole sentence product — with sparsity guaranteeing unseen n-grams everywhere at any n.

Smoothing redistributes probability mass to the unseen: add-one/add-k (crude — steals far too much mass at vocabulary scale), interpolation/backoff (blend or fall back to lower-order models when higher-order counts are thin).

The idea worth remembering: Kneser-Ney — back off not by raw unigram frequency but by continuation probability (how many distinct contexts a word appears in). The "Francisco" example: frequent but only ever after "San", so it deserves low backoff weight. That's the interview answer.

Why n-grams still matter in 2026: they're the cheap fluency signal — autocomplete layers, ASR/spell-correction rescoring, data-quality filters, and the n-gram overlap machinery inside BLEU/ROUGE; plus they're the conceptual baseline neural LMs are measured against (perplexity carries over directly).
One breath of lineage: fixed-window neural LMs → RNNs (unbounded context, vanishing gradients) → attention — the whole arc is "widen the usable context".
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: Without smoothing an unseen n-gram zeroes the whole sentence, so mass gets redistributed — and Kneser-Ney's insight is to back off by how many distinct contexts a word appears in, not raw frequency, which is why 'Francisco' gets almost none.

questions.text: Seq2seq with Bahdanau attention: what bottleneck did attention fix, and how is that the origin story of everything since?
points: The bottleneck: encoder-decoder RNNs compressed the entire source sentence into one fixed-size vector — translation quality degraded sharply with sentence length because the vector saturates; early tricks (reversing input order) were symptoms of the disease.

Attention's fix: keep all encoder states; at each decode step, compute relevance scores of every source position to the current decoder state, softmax them, and read a weighted context vector — the decoder gets random access to the source instead of a summary. Bahdanau = learned additive scoring; Luong = dot-product variants (the direct ancestor of QK-dot-product).

The origin story to tell: attention started as a patch on RNNs; the transformer's move was deleting the RNN and keeping only attention ("attention is all you need") — self-attention as random access within the sequence, parallel across positions. Every modern model is downstream of this one repair.

Bonus fluency: attention weights gave the first useful alignment visualizations (soft word alignment in MT), and cross-attention in today's encoder-decoder and multimodal models is exactly Bahdanau's mechanism, matured.
Decoding strategies ride along: greedy vs beam for MT-class tasks (beam helps constrained generation, causes degeneration in open-ended text — same facts as the LLM pillar, older clothes).
questions.badge: Evergreen — the lineage question that tests whether you understand why transformers exist.
questions.oneLiner: Attention fixed the fixed-vector bottleneck by giving the decoder weighted random access to all encoder states — and the transformer is just that repair promoted to the whole architecture, with the RNN deleted.

questions.text: Why does a CRF beat per-token softmax for NER — and when is the CRF layer still worth adding in 2026?
points: The failure of independent per-token softmax: it can emit structurally invalid sequences — I-PER following B-ORG, I-tags starting entities — because nothing models label-to-label dependencies. BIO/BILOU schemes have hard transition constraints that per-token decisions ignore.

A linear-chain CRF models the joint probability of the whole label sequence: emission scores per token plus learned transition scores between adjacent labels, globally normalized; Viterbi decodes the best valid path. Invalid transitions get effectively forbidden; borderline token decisions get resolved by sequence context.

Lineage one breath deep: HMM (generative, models P(words|tags)) → MEMM (discriminative but suffers label bias from local normalization) → CRF (global normalization fixes label bias) — that progression is a classic interview probe.

2026 relevance: transformer encoders made emissions so good that the CRF's marginal gain shrank — but it still pays where strict schema validity matters (structured extraction feeding databases), on small training sets, and in lightweight non-transformer stacks; the cheap alternative is constrained decoding masks that just forbid invalid transitions.

The framing that generalizes: CRF is structured prediction — enforcing output validity in the model rather than post-hoc — the same idea as constrained decoding for LLM JSON output; drawing that line shows architecture-level understanding.
questions.badge: Trending — CRF-vs-softmax recurs on LeetCode Discuss NLP threads + extraction-heavy JDs (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Per-token softmax can emit I-PER after B-ORG because each decision is independent — a CRF scores whole label paths with learned transitions and Viterbi-decodes the best valid one; today it earns its place where schema validity and small data matter, and it's the same structured-prediction idea as constrained LLM decoding.

questions.text: Viterbi in one minute: what does it compute, and what's the trick that makes it tractable?
points: The problem: find the single most probable tag sequence given observations — naive enumeration is K^T paths (K tags, T tokens), exponential.

The trick is dynamic programming on the Markov property: the best path to tag k at position t only depends on the best paths to each tag at t−1 — so keep, per position, just K best-path scores plus backpointers; recurse forward, then trace back. O(T·K²) instead of K^T.

Say the distinction that filters candidates: Viterbi finds the best joint path (max-product); the forward algorithm computes the total probability over all paths (sum-product) — same recursion, max swapped for sum; posterior per-token marginals need forward-backward.

Where it lives today: CRF/HMM decoding, ASR and spell-correction lattices, any pipeline with chain-structured outputs — and conceptually it's beam search's exact ancestor (beam = approximate Viterbi when the state space is too big to be exact).
If asked to code it: a T×K score table, a backpointer table, careful log-space arithmetic — that's the whole implementation.
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: Viterbi finds the most probable tag path by dynamic programming — the Markov property means the best path to each state at time t needs only the best paths at t−1, collapsing K-to-the-T enumeration into T-by-K-squared with backpointers.

questions.text: Relation extraction and entity linking: what's the difference, and how do you build a knowledge-base population pipeline today?
points: Definitions crisply: NER finds mentions; entity linking disambiguates a mention to a KB identity ("Paris" → city vs person — candidate generation by alias tables, disambiguation by context vs entity descriptions); relation extraction classifies the semantic relation between entity pairs ("works_for", "acquired") — coreference resolution ties mentions across sentences so relations aggregate correctly.

Pipeline shape: document → NER → coreference → entity linking → relation extraction → validation → KB write. Errors cascade — a wrong link poisons every downstream relation — so per-stage precision thresholds and confidence propagation matter more than any single model's F1.

The 2026 build: LLMs do zero/few-shot RE and linking surprisingly well (schema-guided extraction into JSON), but at corpus scale the cost ladder reasserts itself — classical/fine-tuned small models for the bulk, LLM for the hard residual, and always schema-validated output with provenance kept per fact.

The senior warnings: extraction quality is domain-fragile (fine-tune or few-shot on your text, not news benchmarks), and the KB needs entity resolution hygiene (dedup, canonical IDs) or it silently forks entities — the same dedup discipline as everywhere else.
Tie it upward: this pipeline is exactly how the knowledge graphs behind KG-RAG and agent traversal get built — classical NLP is the supply chain of the fancy stuff.
questions.badge: Trending — KB-population questions recur with the KG-RAG wave (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Linking decides which real-world entity a mention is, relation extraction decides how two entities connect — the pipeline cascades NER, coref, linking and RE into a validated KB write, with cheap models for the bulk and LLMs for the hard residual, because this supply chain is what KG-RAG runs on.

questions.text: Extractive vs abstractive summarization: mechanisms, failure modes, and which one you ship for legal documents.
points: Extractive selects existing sentences (TextRank-style graph centrality over sentence similarity, or supervised selection) — output is verbatim-faithful by construction; failure modes are incoherence between stitched sentences and missing cross-sentence synthesis.

Abstractive generates new text (seq2seq → today's LLMs) — fluent, synthesizing, compressible to any length; the failure mode is the deal-breaker: hallucinated content presented as summary — unfaithful claims, subtly shifted numbers/qualifiers.

The legal call: extractive (or extract-then-verify hybrid) — a lawyer can tolerate clunky prose, not an invented qualifier in a liability clause; verbatim traceability to source sentences is itself a requirement (citations = the extractive property).

The production hybrid worth describing: extract candidate spans → LLM rewrites for coherence → faithfulness check (NLI/judge verifying each claim maps to a source span) → render with linked citations; you get fluency with an audit trail.

Evaluation honesty: ROUGE measures n-gram overlap with references, not faithfulness — a fluent hallucination scores fine; faithfulness needs entailment-style checks or human audit, and saying so is the difference between knowing the metric and trusting it.
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: Extractive is faithful by construction but clunky, abstractive is fluent but can invent — so legal gets extract-then-rewrite with per-claim faithfulness checks and linked citations, and ROUGE never decides, because overlap can't see hallucination.

questions.text: Sentiment analysis in production: when does a lexicon (VADER) or a small classifier still beat an LLM call — and what does aspect-based add?
points: The cost ladder is the answer's spine: lexicon (VADER) — zero training, zero inference cost, milliseconds, decent on social-media English (handles negation, intensifiers, emoji heuristically); TF-IDF + logistic regression / small fine-tuned transformer — cheap, fast, domain-tuned (learns that "sick" is positive in sneaker reviews); LLM — best zero-shot quality and nuance (sarcasm, mixed sentiment), orders of magnitude more expensive per document.
The decision variables: volume (millions of documents/day amortize a trained model; LLM bills scale linearly), latency budget, domain drift cadence, and whether you need explanations vs a score.

Streaming/dashboard analytics over social firehoses → classical wins on economics; low-volume, high-stakes, nuanced judgments (exec-escalation triage) → LLM earns it. The hybrid: cheap model scores everything, LLM adjudicates the uncertain band — the cascade pattern again.

Aspect-based sentiment fixes the resolution problem: "food great, service awful" is not "neutral" — extract (aspect, sentiment) pairs so the signal is actionable per dimension; classically a pipeline (aspect extraction + polarity per aspect), today often one schema-guided LLM extraction on sampled data.
The labeling truth: sentiment ground truth is noisy (human agreement is imperfect, sarcasm and mixed cases dominate errors) — report agreement alongside accuracy or the number overpromises.
questions.badge: Trending — the cost-ladder framing recurs in applied-NLP JDs (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: It's a cost ladder — VADER for free at firehose scale, a domain-tuned small classifier for the daily millions, LLMs for the nuanced low-volume band or as adjudicator in a cascade — and aspect-based extraction is what turns 'neutral overall' into 'food great, service awful', which is the signal anyone actually acts on.

questions.text: LDA vs clustering embeddings with BERTopic-style pipelines: how does each find 'topics', and which do you reach for now?
points: LDA's generative story: each document is a mixture of topics (Dirichlet-distributed proportions), each topic a distribution over words; inference reverses the story from observed words. Strengths: documents get soft multi-topic membership, fully interpretable word distributions, no embeddings needed. Weaknesses: bag-of-words blindness to semantics (synonyms split topics), K chosen by hand, notorious instability across runs, and short texts starve it.

Embedding-cluster pipelines (BERTopic-shape): embed documents → reduce (UMAP) → cluster (HDBSCAN) → label clusters by class-based TF-IDF keywords. Strengths: contextual semantics (synonyms merge), no fixed K, handles short text, outliers get a noise bucket. Weaknesses: hard single-assignment by default, stochastic stack (seed sensitivity), and the "topics" are cluster summaries, not a generative model.

Evaluation is the same discipline either way: coherence metrics as a filter, human interpretability as the bar — and the t-SNE/UMAP warnings from the ML pillar apply verbatim to the visualization step.

The 2026 reach: embedding pipelines are the practical default for exploration and voice-of-customer work; LDA survives where you need soft mixtures, a probabilistic model, or auditability of the generative assumptions.
The honest caveat for both: topic models generate hypotheses, not truth — stability across seeds/samples and downstream usefulness are the real tests, same as clustering anywhere.
questions.badge: Evergreen (with a modern second half interviewers now expect)
questions.oneLiner: LDA reverses a generative story — documents as Dirichlet mixtures over word distributions — while BERTopic-style pipelines cluster contextual embeddings and name the clusters; embeddings win the practical default on semantics and short text, LDA keeps soft mixtures and auditability, and both are hypothesis generators judged by stability and use.

bands.name: Section 8 — Information Retrieval & Search (11-Information-Retrieval-Search) — architect core

questions.text: BM25: walk me through the formula's two ideas beyond TF-IDF, and why it's still 'the baseline to beat' in 2026.
points: Idea 1 — term-frequency saturation (k1): TF's contribution is bounded — the 20th occurrence of a term adds almost nothing beyond the 5th (asymptotic curve, not linear or log). Keyword-stuffing stops paying; k1 tunes how quickly the curve flattens.

Idea 2 — length normalization (b): long documents accumulate term matches by sheer bulk — BM25 normalizes TF by document length relative to the corpus average; b dials from no normalization (0) to full (1). Together with IDF, that's the whole formula, conceptually.

Why still the baseline to beat: zero training, interpretable, blazing on inverted indexes at web scale, robust out-of-domain (dense retrievers trained on one distribution degrade on another; BM25 doesn't care), and unbeatable on exact/rare tokens — IDs, code, names, jargon.

The 2026 framing: it's not BM25 vs dense — production retrieval is hybrid (BM25 + dense, fused) because their failure modes are complementary: BM25 misses synonyms/paraphrase, dense misses exact rare strings. Any RAG design answer that drops BM25 entirely is suspect.

Fluency details worth having: default-ish parameters (k1 around 1.2–2, b around 0.75) exist but tuning on your corpus matters; and BM25 scores are corpus-relative — not comparable across indexes without normalization (a fusion gotcha).

questions.badge: Trending — BM25-in-hybrid-retrieval is a fixture of RAG-era screens (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: BM25 adds two ideas to TF-IDF — saturating term frequency so stuffing stops paying, and length normalization so bulk doesn't win — and it's still the baseline because it's free, interpretable, domain-robust, and exact-match-faithful, which is precisely the half of hybrid retrieval dense vectors can't cover.

questions.text: Your semantic search misses exact SKU codes that keyword search finds instantly. Explain, then design the fix.
points: The mechanism: "SKU-X99-4B" carries no distributional semantics — the embedding model fragments it into junk subwords and maps it to a semantically meaningless region; nearest-neighbor search then retrieves by topic vibes, not by the identifier. Dense retrieval is structurally blind to arbitrary exact strings — this isn't a tuning problem.

The fix is hybrid retrieval: a sparse/BM25 arm (inverted index catches exact tokens with high IDF) plus the dense arm (paraphrase and intent), fused — RRF (reciprocal rank fusion) is the robust default because it merges ranks, sidestepping incomparable score scales; weighted score fusion when you've calibrated.

Engineering details that show production experience: keep the identifier fields analyzed minimally in the sparse index (don't stem SKUs), consider field boosts (exact match in title/ID field outranks body), and add a reranker on the fused candidates for final precision.

Detect the failure class systematically: slice your retrieval eval by query type (identifier lookups vs natural-language) — aggregate recall hides that one slice is broken; this is the same slicing discipline as everywhere else.
Say the general law: sparse and dense fail on complementary query classes — which is why the answer to "which retriever?" in production is nearly always "both, fused".

questions.text: MRR, MAP, NDCG, recall@k — which IR metric for which system, and what's the trap in each?
points: Recall@k: fraction of relevant items in the top k — the metric when a downstream stage consumes the whole top-k, which is exactly RAG retrieval (the generator can use anything in context; missing it entirely is the unrecoverable failure). Trap: says nothing about position or precision — fine for RAG, wrong for humans.

MRR: reciprocal rank of the first relevant result — for known-item search and question answering where one hit satisfies (autocomplete, "find the doc"). Trap: blind to everything after the first hit — wrong for multi-answer needs.

MAP: mean of precision at each relevant hit — rewards putting all relevant items high; classic for literature/e-discovery-style search. Trap: assumes binary relevance and users who care about completeness.

NDCG: graded relevance with position discounting — the metric for human-facing ranked pages (web/product search) where "somewhat relevant at rank 2" beats "perfect at rank 9". Trap: needs graded judgments (expensive labels) and the discount curve is a modeling choice.

The system mapping to recite: RAG → recall@k (+ a precision-ish signal if context is tight); QA/known-item → MRR; completeness search → MAP; commercial ranked UX → NDCG. And always with confidence intervals over query sets — per-query variance in IR is huge, and single-number deltas are usually noise.
questions.badge: Evergreen — the metric-selection probe for anything retrieval-shaped.
questions.oneLiner: Match the metric to the consumer: recall@k when an LLM eats the whole top-k, MRR when the first hit satisfies, MAP when completeness matters, NDCG for graded human-facing rankings — and report intervals over the query set, because per-query variance swallows small deltas.

questions.text: Learning to rank: pointwise, pairwise, listwise — what's the actual difference, and where does LTR sit in a modern search stack?
points: Pointwise: regress/classify each (query, doc) relevance independently — simple, but optimizing per-item scores ≠ optimizing the ordering. Pairwise: learn from preferences — doc A above doc B for this query (RankNet lineage) — closer to the goal, dominant in practice (LambdaMART-style gradient-boosted trees remain workhorses). Listwise: optimize a list-level objective approximating NDCG directly (LambdaRank's trick: weight pairwise gradients by their NDCG impact).

Where it sits: the multi-stage funnel — cheap candidate generation (BM25 + dense retrieval, thousands of candidates) → LTR/reranker over hundreds (rich features: text scores, freshness, popularity, personalization, click signals) → optional final neural/cross-encoder rerank over tens. LTR is the feature-fusion stage where business signals join text relevance.

The data reality: labels come from clicks, not judgments, at scale — and clicks carry position bias (people click what's ranked high), so counterfactual/unbiased LTR (propensity weighting) is the difference between learning relevance and learning your old ranker. Same off-policy trap as recommenders.

The 2026 note: cross-encoder/LLM rerankers absorbed the top of the funnel in RAG stacks, but classic feature-based LTR still owns commercial search's middle stage — business features don't live in an embedding.
Interview move: name the funnel and put each technique at its stage — that structure answers most search-design questions by itself.
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: Pointwise scores items, pairwise learns orderings, listwise optimizes the list metric directly — and LTR lives mid-funnel, fusing text scores with business features over candidate sets, trained on click data that must be de-biased for position or you're just relearning the old ranker.

questions.text: BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore: what does each actually measure, and why should none of them gate a release alone?
points: BLEU: n-gram precision against references with a brevity penalty — MT's historical metric; punishes valid paraphrase, blind to meaning-preserving reorderings. ROUGE: n-gram/longest-common-subsequence recall — summarization's historical metric; rewards covering reference content, blind to whether covered content is faithful. BERTScore: token-level embedding similarity — forgives paraphrase, but rewards semantic proximity, which fluently-wrong text also has.

The shared failure that matters: none detects hallucination or factual error — a confident fabrication scores well on all three if it's topically adjacent and fluent. Overlap and similarity are not truth.

Also shared: reference dependence — one or two references can't span the space of valid outputs, so all three systematically undervalue legitimate diversity; scores are comparable only within same-dataset, same-reference setups.

What they're still for: cheap regression tracking during development (did the change move the needle directionally?), corpus-level comparisons of similar systems — as one signal among several, never the gate.

The gating stack (same shape as the LLM pillar): programmatic assertions + faithfulness/entailment checks + calibrated LLM-judge rubrics + sampled human eval — with error analysis by slice, because the aggregate hides which segment broke. Saying "BLEU for the dashboard, judges and humans for the gate" is the expected level.
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: BLEU counts n-gram precision, ROUGE counts recall, BERTScore counts embedding similarity — and all three score a fluent hallucination happily, which is why they track regressions on a dashboard but never gate a release without faithfulness checks and human-calibrated judgment on top.

questions.text: Your NLP model's aggregate F1 went up but users are complaining more. What does your error-analysis discipline look like?
points: Slice first: aggregate F1 is a weighted average that can rise while a user-visible segment collapses — cut by input length, language/dialect, entity type, class, source channel, time period, and user-facing surface. The complaint demographic tells you which slice to cut. Rare-but-critical classes (the safety-relevant intent, the VIP entity type) need their own tracked metrics, or the average launders their failure.

Significance second: was the F1 gain real? Bootstrap the test set for intervals; paired tests on per-example outcomes for model comparisons — the same discipline as the ML pillar, applied to text. Small deltas on modest eval sets are routinely noise.

Read the errors: sample false positives/negatives per slice and categorize by hand — annotation errors, genuine ambiguity, preprocessing bugs, distribution shift, systematic model blind spots. A hundred hand-read errors beat another metric; the categories become the roadmap.

Check eval-production mismatch: your test set is last year's distribution — complaints may reflect drift the frozen eval can't see. Sample production traffic, label it fresh, compare against the static set.
Institutionalize: slice dashboards in every eval report, a "no launch if any protected slice regresses" rule, and complaint-to-eval-case triage — the flywheel again.
questions.badge: Trending — slicing-and-significance questions recur across applied-NLP screens (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Aggregate F1 launders slice failures and small deltas are often bootstrap noise — so I slice by segment and surface, test significance on paired outcomes, hand-categorize a sample of errors, and re-label fresh production traffic, because the complaint stream is telling me which of those the frozen eval missed.

questions.text: You have 400 labeled examples and a deadline. Walk me through augmentation and weak supervision — and their failure modes.
points: Augmentation transforms existing examples: synonym/word swaps (EDA-style), back-translation (round-trip through another language for natural paraphrase), and today LLM paraphrase/generation — the strongest option, generating labeled variants or entirely synthetic examples from class descriptions.

Augmentation's failure mode: label-breaking transforms — a synonym swap flips sentiment ("not bad"→"not good"-class bugs), paraphrase drifts across class boundaries; augment conservatively on tasks where meaning is label-critical, and spot-check a sample by hand.

Weak supervision (Snorkel-shape): write labeling functions — heuristics, keyword rules, distant supervision from KBs, model votes — and combine their noisy votes into probabilistic labels via a label model that learns each function's accuracy and correlations. Scales labels without annotators; failure mode is correlated noise — functions sharing a bias fool the combiner into confident wrong labels.

The LLM-era twist: LLM-as-annotator is now the dominant weak-labeler — cheap bulk labeling, but audit against a human-labeled gold slice (biases are systematic, not random, so they don't wash out), then train a small fast model on the LLM labels — distillation of judgment into economics.
The discipline regardless of method: keep a human-labeled, untouched eval set — synthetic anything in the eval set and you're grading the generator, not the model.
questions.badge: Trending — low-label-budget scenarios recur on applied-NLP screens (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Augment with back-translation or LLM paraphrase but spot-check for label-breaking transforms, weak-supervise with labeling functions or LLM annotation audited against a human gold slice — and keep the eval set human-labeled and synthetic-free, or you're measuring the generator.

questions.text: Your English-trained pipeline hits Hinglish, emoji-dense, code-mixed support tickets. What breaks, and what's the triage?
points: Language identification breaks first: LID assumes monolingual documents; code-mixed text ("yaar this app is bakwas") confuses document-level detectors — you need token/span-level LID or a router that has a code-mixed class at all. Misrouted text then hits the wrong everything downstream.

Tokenization/normalization breaks quietly: romanized Hindi has no canonical spelling ("bahut/bohot/bht"), emoji and elongations ("sooooo") explode variants; English-centric subword vocabs fragment it into junk — the same tokenizer-inequity mechanics as the LLM pillar, now at pipeline scale.

Model triage ladder: multilingual pretrained models (XLM-R-class, or multilingual LLMs) handle code-mixing far better than translate-then-process (translation destroys the mixing signal itself, and MT on noisy romanized input is garbage-in anyway); fine-tune on your actual tickets — a few thousand in-domain code-mixed labels beat any amount of clean-English data.

Evaluation must be sliced by language mix — aggregate metrics hide that the Hinglish slice is at chance; build a labeled eval slice per major mix, and monitor the mix distribution over time (it drifts with your user base).

The architect's framing: multilingual isn't a model choice, it's a pipeline audit — LID, normalization policy, vocab coverage, labeled slices, and a fallback route (low-confidence → human or LLM) per stage.
questions.badge: Trending — code-mixing/noisy-text questions recur in global-product JDs (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Code-mixed text breaks LID first, then the tokenizer, then every English assumption downstream — the fix is span-level LID, minimal normalization, a multilingual model fine-tuned on your real tickets rather than translate-then-process, and eval slices per language mix so the failure can't hide in the aggregate.

questions.text: Design the text pipeline that deduplicates a billion documents and strips PII — the algorithms, not the buzzwords.
points: Exact dedup: normalize → hash (content fingerprint) → drop collisions. Trivial and insufficient — the web's duplication is near-duplication (boilerplate variants, timestamps, minor edits).

Near-dup at scale = MinHash + LSH: shingle documents (word/char n-grams) → MinHash signatures (k independent min-hashes approximate Jaccard similarity in compact form) → LSH banding hashes signature bands into buckets so documents above a similarity threshold collide with high probability — candidate pairs come from shared buckets only, turning O(n²) comparison into near-linear. Band/row parameters tune the similarity threshold's S-curve. That's the answer they're probing for.

Verify candidates with exact Jaccard/edit checks; cluster and keep one canonical doc per group (provenance retained). Semantic near-dup (paraphrased duplicates) → embedding-cluster dedup as a second pass, budget permitting.

PII layering: regex/validators for structured PII (emails, phones, cards — with checksum validation to cut false positives), NER-based detection for names/addresses/orgs, context rules for ambiguity (a name in a byline vs in a medical record), then policy per class: drop, mask, or pseudonymize consistently (same entity → same token, preserving utility). Measure both precision and recall on a labeled audit slice — silent PII leakage is the asymmetric risk.

Pipeline hygiene: idempotent stages, sampled QA at every stage, and stats dashboards (dedup rate, PII hit rate per class) — a sudden shift in either is an upstream-change alarm. This exact pipeline is also LLM-pretraining data discipline — same machinery, higher stakes.

questions.badge: Trending — MinHash/dedup questions recur in data-engineering-for-AI JDs (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Exact hashing catches identical docs; near-dup needs MinHash signatures approximating Jaccard plus LSH banding so similar documents collide into candidate buckets — near-linear instead of quadratic — and PII gets layered regex-plus-NER detection with consistent pseudonymization, both audited on labeled slices because silent leakage is the asymmetric failure.

questions.text: Design a text-classification system from zero labels to production — the cold-start, the labeling budget, and the retraining loop.
points: Phase 1, zero labels: ship a baseline this week — rules/keywords for the obvious classes, or LLM zero-shot classification as the cold-start model (expensive per call but instant coverage); either way it's simultaneously your first labeling machine, generating weak labels + surfacing the taxonomy's real shape (classes always change once real data arrives).

Phase 2, spend the budget smartly: human labels go where they're worth most — active learning (label what the current model is least certain about), disagreement sampling (where LLM and rules disagree), and per-class coverage floors for rare classes. Build the gold eval set first — a small trusted eval beats more training labels for decision-making.

Phase 3, the economic swap: distill to a small fast model (fine-tuned transformer or even TF-IDF+LR for high-volume) trained on accumulated labels — LLM cost at cold start, classical economics at scale; keep the LLM as fallback for low-confidence and as a periodic auditor.

The retraining loop: production sampling → labeling queue → drift monitors (input distribution, class balance, confidence histograms) → scheduled or triggered retrain through the same eval gate; taxonomy evolution (new classes appearing) is the change that breaks silently, so watch the "other/low-confidence" bucket's growth rate.
Throughout: confidence thresholds route uncertain traffic to humans — the system is a cascade with a human floor, not a lone classifier.

questions.oneLiner: Cold-start with rules or LLM zero-shot to ship and generate weak labels, spend human labels on a gold eval set plus active-learning picks, distill to a cheap model at volume with the LLM as low-confidence fallback — and keep it alive with drift monitors and a watched other-bucket, because taxonomies rot before models do.

questions.text: Design search with autocomplete for a product catalog — indexing, ranking layers, and the latency budget.
points: Two systems: autocomplete fires per keystroke — single-digit-to-tens of ms, served from prefix structures (tries/FSTs, or edge-n-gram indexes) over queries and product names, ranked by popularity + personalization priors, with fuzzy tolerance for typos (edit-distance-bounded). Search fires on submit — a ~100–300 ms budget through the full funnel.

Indexing: inverted index with per-field analyzers (minimal analysis on SKUs/brand, standard on descriptions — the Q17 lesson), plus a dense embedding index for semantic recall; near-real-time index updates for price/stock (staleness here is a business bug, not a relevance bug).

Ranking funnel: candidate generation (BM25 + dense, union via RRF; thousands) → LTR mid-stage fusing text scores with business features (popularity, margin, stock, personalization; hundreds) → optional cross-encoder top-k polish (tens) — each stage 10x cheaper per doc than the next, which is the whole point of the funnel.

Query understanding on the way in: spell-correction (noisy-channel/edit distance), LID if multilingual, category/intent detection routing ("red nike shoes size 10" → filters + text), synonym expansion on the sparse arm.

Evaluation and feedback: offline NDCG on judged sets sliced by query type (head vs tail vs identifier), online CTR/conversion A/Bs, and click-through feeding LTR with position-bias correction — the loop from Q19. Zero-result-rate and reformulation-rate are the underrated health metrics.

questions.text: Design a content-moderation pipeline where precision-recall tuning is a business decision, not a modeling detail.
points: The business framing first: each category has its own cost asymmetry — CSAM/violence: recall at almost any precision cost (a miss is catastrophic, an over-block is an apology); borderline spam: precision-lean (over-blocking legitimate users bleeds the platform). So thresholds are set per category by policy owners against measured FP/FN costs, not globally by F1 — that reframing is the question's point.

The cascade for economics: cheap always-on layers (hash-matching against known-bad content, keyword/regex, lightweight classifiers) filter the firehose; heavier models (transformers, multimodal for image+text) score the residual; LLM or human judgment for the ambiguous band. Volume drops orders of magnitude per stage — the only way moderation scales.

Humans by design: uncertain-band review queues with severity-based SLAs, appeal flows (an appeals overturn rate is your FP monitor), and reviewer wellbeing engineering (exposure limits, blurring) — mention it; it's a real architectural constraint.

Adversarial reality: evasion evolves (leetspeak, re-encoding, image-text smuggling) — so normalization layers, continuous red-teaming, fresh-labeled drift monitoring, and fast rule-deployment paths for emerging patterns; moderation is a pursuit, not a model.

Metrics that matter: per-category precision/recall on fresh labeled samples, prevalence (what slips through, measured by random-sample audit — not by what gets reported), time-to-action by severity, appeal overturn rates. Prevalence-by-audit is the honest north star, and knowing that separates practitioners from tourists.

questions.text: Give me your cost-latency-quality framework for 'classical NLP vs LLM API' — the one you'd actually run a decision through.
points: The economics line: classical has training cost but near-zero marginal cost; LLM APIs are the inverse — so the decision pivot is volume × lifetime: millions of documents daily for years → the trained model's economics are untouchable; hundreds daily or a two-month project → API wins on engineering time alone. Latency mirrors it: microseconds-to-ms (classical) vs hundreds of ms (API) — real-time paths (autocomplete, inline moderation) often can't take an LLM call.

The task-shape line: fixed-taxonomy, high-volume, stable tasks (classification, NER on known types, dedup, search scoring) are classical territory — quality parity at a fraction of the cost once you have labels; open-ended generation, reasoning, zero-shot flexibility, and long-tail nuance are LLM territory where classical simply can't play.

The data line: no labels and need it now → LLM; labels exist or can be distilled (LLM labels → small model, Q25's swap) → classical inherits the quality at classical prices. Distillation is the bridge that makes this a lifecycle, not a fork.

The default architecture is the cascade: cheap model handles the confident bulk, LLM takes the uncertain band and the audit role — you buy LLM quality at near-classical average cost; plus governance factors (on-prem/PII → local classical or self-hosted; provider dependency risk) as tiebreakers.

Re-run the numbers periodically: API prices fall, small open models improve — the frontier between the territories moves yearly, and last year's build-vs-call answer expires like the self-hosting one.

questions.oneLiner: Volume times lifetime sets the economics, task shape sets the capability boundary, and label availability sets the path — with distillation converting LLM judgment into classical economics and the cascade buying LLM quality at bulk-classical prices, re-priced yearly because the frontier moves.

questions.text: Embedding infrastructure: versioning, ANN serving, and drift — what does mature embedding ops look like?
points: The cardinal rule: query and document vectors must come from the same model version — vectors from different models (or versions) live in incompatible spaces, and mixed-version similarity is silent garbage. Version-tag every vector and every index; enforce compatibility at query time, not by convention.

Upgrades mean re-embedding the corpus: an embedding-model change forces full corpus re-embedding into a new index, blue-green swapped after side-by-side retrieval eval (recall@k on your golden queries, old vs new) — never in-place drift between spaces. That re-embedding cost is why embedding-model churn is an architectural decision, not a pip upgrade.

ANN serving trade-offs: HNSW-class indexes trade recall against latency/memory via build and search parameters — measure ANN recall against exact search on your data (the index introduces its own miss rate on top of the model's); watch index freshness (streaming upserts vs periodic rebuilds, tombstone accumulation), and filters (pre vs post-filtering changes both latency and effective recall).

Drift monitoring: input-text distribution drift (new domains fragment differently), retrieval-quality drift (golden-query recall tracked over time), and usage drift (query length/type mix). Embedding spaces don't drift by themselves — your data drifts around a frozen model, which shows up as slowly decaying retrieval metrics.

Operational completeness: vector-store cost scales with dimensions × corpus (dimension choice and quantized/compressed vectors are real levers), per-tenant isolation for multi-tenant indexes, and deletion compliance (vectors of deleted source docs must go too — vectors are data).

questions.badge: Trending — embedding-ops questions recur in RAG-platform JDs (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: One embedding space per index, version-enforced at query time; model upgrades mean re-embed-everything into a blue-green index gated by golden-query recall; ANN parameters are a measured recall-latency trade on your data; and drift is your corpus moving around a frozen model, caught by tracked retrieval metrics — plus remembering vectors are data with deletion obligations.

questions.text: Extractive, abstractive, open-domain QA — map the lineage from SQuAD-era systems to RAG.
points: Extractive QA: answer is a span in a given passage — model predicts start/end positions (BERT-era SQuAD systems); precise, citable, cheap, but can't synthesize across passages or answer anything not verbatim present.
Abstractive QA: generate the answer in natural language — handles synthesis and phrasing, inherits the hallucination risk; quality became an LLM story.

Open-domain QA: no passage given — retrieve then read: sparse (BM25) then dense retrieval (DPR lineage — bi-encoders trained for QA relevance) feeding a reader/generator. Say the punchline: open-domain QA with a generative reader is RAG — the RAG paper literally formalized retriever+generator; today's stacks are this architecture scaled.

What each era contributed to the modern stack: extractive left span-grounding and citations, DPR left trained retrievers and hard-negative discipline, abstractive left the generator — a modern RAG answer with cited spans is all three eras composed.

Evaluation carried over too: exact-match/F1 from SQuAD for short answers, retrieval recall@k for the retriever stage, faithfulness checks for the generated layer — the metric per stage, not one number.

questions.badge: Evergreen (the lineage version is how it's asked now)
questions.oneLiner: Extractive points at a span, abstractive writes the answer, open-domain retrieves first — and retrieve-then-generate open-domain QA is literally RAG's origin, with modern stacks composing all three eras: trained retrieval, generated answers, span-grounded citations.

questions.text: What did machine translation teach NLP? Walk the SMT→NMT arc and name the lessons that generalized.
points: SMT era: translation as noisy-channel decoding — phrase tables (learned alignments), a language model for fluency, log-linear feature combination, beam-search decoding. Powerful, but a pipeline of separately-trained pieces with hand-tuned glue.

NMT: one end-to-end seq2seq network — first RNN encoder-decoder (the fixed-vector bottleneck), then attention (invented for MT, Q9), then the transformer (built for MT — the original paper's task). Quality jumped, the pipeline collapsed into one model.

Lessons that generalized: subword tokenization (BPE entered NLP through NMT's open-vocabulary problem), attention → the universal mechanism, beam search + its degeneration quirks, BLEU and the whole reference-based-metric debate, back-translation as augmentation (Q22), and the meta-lesson — end-to-end learning beats hand-assembled pipelines when data suffices — which is the LLM thesis in miniature.

Today's state: MT is largely an LLM capability (translation as prompting), with dedicated NMT systems surviving on cost at massive scale and in low-resource specialization; low-resource languages remain the honest frontier (data scarcity, evaluation scarcity).
Interview positioning: MT history answers "why is the field shaped like this" — attention, subwords, BLEU skepticism, and end-to-end-ism all trace to one task's pressure.
questions.badge: Evergreen (MT is the field's history exam — and its lessons are current events)
questions.oneLiner: MT went from noisy-channel phrase pipelines to end-to-end seq2seq, inventing attention, mainstreaming BPE and back-translation, and teaching the field that end-to-end beats assembled pipelines given data — the transformer itself was built for translation, so modern NLP is MT's lessons generalized.

questions.text: Neural LM lineage: fixed-window → RNN → LSTM → attention. What killed each stage?
points: Fixed-window neural LMs (Bengio-lineage): embed n previous words, MLP predicts the next — proved distributed representations beat count-based sparsity, died of the hard context window (n fixed, no long dependencies) and parameter growth with window size.

Vanilla RNNs: recurrence gives unbounded context in principle — died of vanishing/exploding gradients: error signal decays across timesteps, so "unbounded" context was theoretical; long dependencies untrainable.

LSTMs/GRUs: gating (input/forget/output) creates a protected cell-state highway for gradients — genuinely fixed trainability at range, ruled for a decade — died of sequential computation: each step waits for the previous, so no parallelism across the sequence during training; long-range information still degrades through repeated state compression.

Attention/transformers: direct position-to-position connections — path length 1 between any tokens (vs n for recurrence), fully parallel training — traded it for O(n²) cost, which is the constraint the current era engineers around (the LLM pillar's whole serving section).

The pattern worth voicing: each transition solved the predecessor's training bottleneck (capacity → gradients → parallelism) — and the SSM/Mamba conversation is the same loop attacking the transformer's quadratic term; history hasn't stopped.
questions.badge: Evergreen — the "do you know why, not just what" architecture-history probe.
questions.oneLiner: Fixed windows died of the hard context limit, RNNs of vanishing gradients, LSTMs — after gating fixed trainability — of sequential non-parallelism, and transformers bought parallel training and unit path-length at quadratic cost, which is exactly the term today's SSM work is trying to kill next.

questions.text: Constituency vs dependency parsing — and who actually consumes a parse tree in 2026?
points: Constituency parsing: nested phrase structure (NP/VP trees) from a grammar — linguistics-native, the classic representation for syntactic theory. Dependency parsing: directed head→dependent arcs with typed relations (nsubj, dobj) — flatter, word-centric, cross-lingually more natural, and far more usable programmatically ("find the subject of this verb" is one arc lookup).

Dependency won the applied war: spaCy-class pipelines ship dependency parses; typical consumers today — rule-based extraction in high-precision domains (legal/biomedical patterns over arcs beat black-box recall when a miss is expensive), aspect-sentiment linking ("battery" ← "terrible"), query understanding, and linguistically-informed feature engineering where training data is scarce.

The honest 2026 status: transformers learn syntax implicitly (probing finds it in attention/representations), so explicit parsing vanished from most neural pipelines — parses survive where you need inspectable, guaranteed structure (auditability, rules) rather than implicit competence.

The evaluation vocabulary if probed: labeled/unlabeled attachment score (LAS/UAS) for dependencies; and transition-based vs graph-based parsers as the two algorithm families — one sentence each is enough.

Frame it as the recurring theme: explicit structure vs learned competence — the same trade as CRF-vs-softmax and rules-vs-LLM; classical structure survives at the precision-and-audit end of every one of these.
questions.badge: Evergreen (tests whether classical knowledge comes with honest currency)
questions.oneLiner: Constituency nests phrases, dependency draws typed head-to-dependent arcs — dependency won production because arcs are queryable — and in 2026 parses survive where inspectable structure beats implicit competence: high-precision rule extraction, aspect linking, and anywhere audit matters more than recall.

questions.text: WSD, SRL, coreference — the classical semantic tasks. Which did LLMs absorb, and what's left standing?
points: The tasks in one line each: WSD — which sense of "bank" is this occurrence; SRL — who did what to whom (predicate-argument structure: agent, patient, instrument); coreference — which mentions refer to the same entity across a text.

WSD got absorbed almost completely: contextual embeddings are sense disambiguation — every token vector is already context-conditioned; nobody ships a standalone WSD component anymore. It survives as a probe task and in lexicography.

SRL mostly absorbed as competence, but survives as explicit structure where downstream systems consume frames — event extraction in finance/pharma ("who acquired whom for how much"), where you want typed, schema-validated outputs rather than prose understanding. Increasingly done by schema-guided LLM extraction — the task survives, the dedicated model rarely.

Coreference is the survivor: KB population and entity-centric pipelines (Q12) need explicit mention clusters — aggregating facts per entity requires knowing which "he/the company/Apple" corefer; long-document coref remains genuinely imperfect even for LLMs, and errors cascade into every entity-level aggregate.

The pattern to state: semantic tasks survived in proportion to whether their output is consumed by machines — implicit competence killed the human-invisible ones; explicit-structure consumers keep the rest alive as extraction schemas.
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: WSD dissolved into contextual embeddings, SRL survives as schema-guided event extraction where machines consume the frames, and coreference is the real survivor because entity-centric pipelines need explicit mention clusters — the rule being that a semantic task outlives absorption only if something downstream eats its structure.

questions.text: You need a labeled corpus for a new task. Walk me through annotation design — guidelines, agreement, and the metrics that tell you the labels are usable.
points: Guidelines are developed, not written: draft → pilot round on a shared sample → adjudicate disagreements → revise the guidelines with the hard cases as examples → repeat until agreement stabilizes. Most label noise is guideline ambiguity, not annotator carelessness — edge-case rulings in the doc are the asset.

Measure chance-corrected agreement: raw percent agreement flatters (two annotators agreeing 85% on a 90/10 skewed binary task is barely better than chance) — use Cohen's kappa (two annotators), Fleiss/Krippendorff (multiple/missing) — and report it per class; aggregate kappa hides that one confusing class is unlabelable.

Agreement is your model's ceiling: if humans agree at 0.7 kappa, a model "beating" the implied accuracy is fitting annotator noise — and your eval set's error bars are bounded by label quality, which is why the gold set gets multiple annotations + adjudication while bulk training data can be single-passed.

Disagreement is signal: systematic disagreement flags genuinely ambiguous classes (merge them, or model soft labels), and per-annotator drift/bias monitoring (against gold-seeded items) keeps a long-running effort honest.

LLM-era addendum: LLM pre-annotation with human correction cuts cost dramatically — but measure human-LLM agreement the same way, and never let the LLM define the gold standard it will later be judged against.
questions.badge: Trending — annotation-quality questions recur as eval-set building became core work (2025–26)
questions.oneLiner: Iterate guidelines through pilot-adjudicate-revise cycles until chance-corrected agreement stabilizes, report kappa per class, and treat human agreement as the model's ceiling and the eval set's error bar — with disagreement mined as signal, because most label noise is guideline ambiguity wearing an annotator's name.

questions.text: NLTK vs spaCy vs Hugging Face — the library-selection answer for a production system.
points: NLTK: the pedagogical toolkit — every classical algorithm implemented readably, corpora included; right for teaching, prototyping a classical idea, linguistics research. Wrong for production: slow, no unified pipeline, aging maintenance.

spaCy: the production pipeline — fast (Cython), one opinionated API (tokenize→tag→parse→NER in a single nlp() call), pretrained per-language pipelines, built for throughput and deployment (batching, GPU, serialization). The default when you need classical outputs (entities, deps, tokens) at volume.

Hugging Face: the model hub + transformers runtime — any pretrained transformer, fine-tuning infrastructure, tokenizers, datasets. The default when the task needs learned quality over pipeline speed, or any custom fine-tune.

The stacking reality: production systems combine them — spaCy for fast structural preprocessing and rule layers (its transformer-backed pipelines literally wrap HF models), HF for the fine-tuned heavy lifting, NLTK nowhere near prod. Choosing is about the layer, not the brand.

Selection heuristics to say: throughput-critical + standard outputs → spaCy; custom learned task → HF; and evaluate pretrained pipeline accuracy on your domain before trusting either — news-trained NER on clinical text embarrasses everyone.

questions.oneLiner: NLTK teaches, spaCy ships classical pipelines fast, Hugging Face supplies and fine-tunes the transformers — production stacks layer spaCy's structure and rules over HF's models, and the real decision is which layer your requirement lives in, checked against your domain's accuracy, not the library's fame.

questions.text: When are BoW/n-gram features still the right representation in 2026 — not the fallback, the right call?
points: Interpretability as a requirement: TF-IDF + linear model gives per-feature coefficients a regulator or auditor can read — "flagged because 'wire transfer' + 'urgent'" — model-risk teams in finance/health accept that where they'd fight an embedding. Not a consolation prize; a spec.

Exact-token fidelity: codes, IDs, jargon, rare names — the same property that keeps BM25 alive (Q16/Q17) makes sparse features right for matching-flavored classification (routing by product code, log-line triage).

Economics at extreme volume: microsecond CPU inference, no GPU, trivially shardable — for a billion-events-a-day filter where the task is lexically separable, spending embedding compute is engineering vanity.

Tiny-data and drift-transparency regimes: with hundreds of labels, TF-IDF+LR's low variance often beats fine-tuning; and when the input distribution shifts, sparse-feature drift is legible (new vocabulary appears, coefficients inspectable) versus silent embedding-space rot.

The test to apply: is the task lexically separable (surface words decide) or semantically separable (meaning beyond surface decides)? Spam/routing/log-triage lean lexical; intent/nuance/paraphrase lean semantic. Run the cheap baseline first — it prices the problem, same discipline as the ML pillar's logistic-regression rule.
questions.badge: Evergreen (the anti-hype judgment question)
questions.oneLiner: Sparse features are the right call when the requirement is interpretability, exact-token fidelity, microsecond economics, or tiny-data stability — the test is whether the task is lexically or semantically separable, and the TF-IDF baseline is what tells you, which is why it always runs first.

questions.text: Spelling correction with the noisy-channel model — the mechanism, and where this exact pattern shows up elsewhere.
points: The noisy-channel frame: observed misspelling x, find intended word w maximizing P(w|x) ∝ P(x|w) · P(w) — an error model (how likely is this typo given that word — keyboard adjacency, phonetic confusion, edit operations) times a language model prior (how likely is the word, ideally in context: "a peace of cake" needs context to fix, since "peace" is a fine word).

Candidate generation bounds the search: words within edit distance 1–2 (insert/delete/substitute/transpose — Damerau-Levenshtein), or phonetic keys (Soundex-family) for sound-alike errors; then the channel model ranks candidates.

The two error classes worth naming: non-word errors (easy to detect — not in vocabulary) vs real-word errors ("their/there") — the second is undetectable without the contextual prior, which is why context-free spellcheckers miss them.

Where the pattern recurs — the answer's payoff: ASR (acoustic model × language model), SMT (translation model × LM — Q31), OCR post-correction, and query correction in search ("did you mean") with click-throughs as training data for the error model. Noisy-channel is Bayes' rule as systems architecture.

Modern status: transformers do correction implicitly (and LLMs do it zero-shot), but the noisy-channel decomposition survives in autocomplete/search stacks for its speed and its tunability — you can adjust the error model without touching the prior.
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: Noisy-channel correction maximizes an error model times a language-model prior over edit-distance candidates — real-word errors force the prior to be contextual — and the same Bayes decomposition is the architecture of ASR, classical MT, and search's did-you-mean, which is why it's worth knowing beyond spellcheck.

questions.text: How do you evaluate an embedding model before betting a retrieval system on it — intrinsic vs extrinsic, and the traps?
points: Intrinsic evals: similarity/analogy benchmarks for the static era; STS correlation and public retrieval suites (MTEB-class) for sentence embeddings — useful as a shortlist filter, cheap to run, and increasingly gamed/overfit as leaderboards mature (the same contamination-and-mismatch caveats as LLM benchmarks, Q40 of the LLM drill).

Extrinsic = your task: build a golden set of your real queries against your real corpus (labeled relevant docs), measure recall@k/MRR per query type — identifier lookups, paraphrase queries, long questions — because models rank differently per slice, and your traffic mix decides the winner.

The traps: domain shift (a general-web champion fumbles clinical or legalese — check vocabulary fragmentation on your corpus as a cheap proxy); usage-convention mismatch (query/passage prefixes, max sequence length truncating your documents silently, pooling choice); metric mismatch with your ANN index (Q5); and dimension-cost coupling — a slightly-better 3072-dim model doubles vector-store cost versus 1536, which at corpus scale is real money against marginal recall.

Run the bake-off properly: same corpus, same chunking, same index parameters, several candidate models, sliced results with intervals — an afternoon of harness work that regularly overturns the leaderboard ordering.
Remember the system view: embedding quality is one stage — a mediocre embedder plus a reranker often beats a great embedder alone on final precision; evaluate the pipeline, then attribute.
