questions.oneLiner: Intrinsic benchmarks shortlist, but only recall-at-k on your own queries against your own corpus — sliced by query type, with prefixes, truncation, metric and dimension-cost checked — predicts the system, and the bake-off harness that proves it is an afternoon that routinely overturns the leaderboard.

questions.text: Paraphrase detection and semantic near-duplicates: how do you build it at scale, and where does it earn money?
points: The task ladder: semantic textual similarity (graded 0–5 relatedness) vs paraphrase detection (binary same-meaning) vs entailment/NLI (directional — "A implies B" isn't symmetric); knowing which your product needs prevents building the wrong classifier (duplicate-question detection is paraphrase; contradiction-flagging is NLI).

The scale architecture is bi-encoder recall + cross-encoder precision: embed everything, ANN-search candidate pairs above a similarity floor (this replaces MinHash when duplication is semantic), then a cross-encoder (joint encoding of the pair — far more accurate than vector cosine, far too slow for all-pairs) adjudicates candidates. The two-stage pattern is this pillar's recurring funnel, once more.

Threshold discipline: cosine cut-offs are corpus- and model-relative — calibrate on a labeled pair set per deployment, and expect the hard band (same topic, different claims) to need the cross-encoder or human review; that band is where cosine lies most.

Where it earns money: duplicate-question/ticket merging (support deflection), training-and-eval-set decontamination (semantic leakage that exact hashing misses — Q7 of the LLM drill at your scale), plagiarism and content-farm detection, moderation recidivism (reposting banned content reworded — Q27's adversarial loop), and news/feed clustering.
The adversarial caveat: paraphrase evasion is deliberate in moderation contexts — monitor the miss rate on reworded-known-bad samples, not just STS benchmarks.
questions.badge: Evergreen
questions.oneLiner: Semantic dedup swaps MinHash for a bi-encoder-ANN recall stage with a cross-encoder precision stage on the candidates, thresholds calibrated on your own labeled pairs — and it earns its keep in ticket merging, eval decontamination, and catching banned content that came back reworded.

questions.text: HMMs for tagging: the generative story, its two assumptions, and why discriminative models replaced it.
points: The generative story: walk a Markov chain of hidden tags (transition probabilities P(tag|previous tag)), and at each tag emit a word (emission probabilities P(word|tag)) — the sentence is the emitted sequence; tagging inverts the story with Bayes + Viterbi (Q11).

The two assumptions: Markov on tags (next tag depends only on the previous — defensible-ish) and emission independence (a word depends only on its own tag, not on neighbors or other words — linguistically absurd, and the model's real ceiling).

Why discriminative won: an HMM models the joint P(words, tags) — wasteful, you never need to generate sentences — and its emission structure can't absorb rich overlapping features (capitalization, suffixes, word shape, embeddings). Discriminative models (MEMM → CRF, Q10) model P(tags|words) directly and eat arbitrary features of the whole observed sentence.

The generalizable lesson to voice: model the conditional you actually need — generative models pay for modeling inputs they'll never predict; the same argument shape appears everywhere from naive Bayes-vs-logistic to why nobody tags with LLM generation when a discriminative head is cheaper and calibrated.

HMMs' residual value: unsupervised/low-resource settings (EM over unlabeled text), and as the cleanest teaching case for latent-variable inference — plus their machinery (Viterbi, forward-backward) outlived the model itself.
questions.badge: Evergreen — the generative-vs-discriminative probe, POS edition.
questions.oneLiner: An HMM generates tags by Markov chain and words by per-tag emission — tractable because of two independence assumptions, one absurd — and CRFs replaced it by modeling the conditional you actually need over rich whole-sentence features, while its Viterbi machinery outlived it everywhere.

questions.text: CNNs for text had a moment. What were they good at, why did transformers displace them, and what survived?
points: The mechanism: 1-D convolutions over word-embedding sequences — each filter is a learned n-gram detector (a width-3 filter learns to fire on "not very good"-shaped trigrams); max-pooling asks "did this pattern appear anywhere"; stacked widths capture multiple n-gram sizes. Kim-CNN-era text classification.

Why they worked: parallel (unlike RNNs of the same era), fast, strong at local-pattern tasks — sentiment, spam, intent — where a few key phrases decide the label; position-invariance via pooling matched the "pattern anywhere" nature of classification.

The structural limit: a fixed receptive field — long-range dependencies need depth (dilated stacks) and arrive degraded; no content-based routing between distant positions, which is exactly what attention provides natively. Transformers displaced them on quality; pretrained transformers made task-specific architectures mostly moot.

What survived: the efficiency niche — character-CNNs inside fastText-era systems, edge/embedded classification at microsecond budgets, and convolutional components inside hybrid architectures; conceptually, "learned local pattern detector" survives as the intuition for early transformer layers and for why small local-window models still price well on lexical tasks (Q37's territory).

Interview use: the CNN story is a clean example of the recurring trade — inductive bias for efficiency vs generality for quality — worth telling in one breath when asked "why did architecture X lose".
questions.badge: Evergreen (era-literacy; occasionally a genuine efficiency question)
questions.oneLiner: Text CNNs learned n-gram detectors with pooling asking 'did the pattern appear anywhere' — fast and strong for local-pattern classification, structurally blind to long range, displaced by attention's content-based routing — surviving in efficiency niches and as the cleanest parable of inductive bias versus generality.

questions.text: Levels of linguistic analysis and the task taxonomy — the 30-second map of the whole field.
points: The levels, climbing: morphology (word-internal structure — inflection, derivation), syntax (how words combine — the parse layer), semantics (literal meaning — senses, roles, relations), pragmatics/discourse (meaning in context — coreference, coherence, intent, irony). Phonology below if speech. Each classical subfield (Q1–Q41) sits at one level; ambiguity at every level is why NLP is hard in one word.

The task taxonomy by output type: text → label (classification, sentiment), text → spans/structure (NER, parsing, extraction), text → text (translation, summarization, QA), text pair → judgment (similarity, NLI), text → ranking (retrieval). Five shapes cover essentially everything, and each shape carries its own metric family and system pattern — which is why the taxonomy is useful, not just tidy.

The unifying 2026 observation: LLMs collapsed the modeling across the taxonomy (everything is text→text with the right prompt), but the shapes still govern evaluation and architecture — a ranking task still needs ranking metrics and a funnel, whatever model sits inside.

Use it as an interview instrument: when handed a vague NLP problem, classify it into a shape out loud — the metric, baseline, and system design follow almost mechanically; that move visibly organizes an answer.
questions.badge: Evergreen — the warm-up that reveals whether your knowledge has a skeleton.
questions.oneLiner: Morphology up through syntax, semantics and discourse — with ambiguity at every level being the field's whole difficulty — and every task maps text to one of five output shapes, which still dictate metrics and architecture even now that one model family serves them all.

questions.text: Three eras of NLP — rules, statistics, neural. What did each era get right that the next one kept?
points: Rule era (grammars, lexicons, hand-built pipelines): got right that language has structure worth encoding — its inheritance is the precision layer that never died: regex and pattern rules in every production system (Q27's cascade floor, Q33's extraction), gazetteer features, and the guardrail habit of deterministic checks around stochastic cores.

Statistical era (counts, probabilistic models, feature engineering): got right that learning from corpora beats hand-encoding at scale, and left the durable machinery — the noisy-channel frame (Q38), evaluation discipline (held-out sets, agreement metrics, significance — Q21/Q35), TF-IDF/BM25 (Q16), and the entire habit of measuring instead of asserting.

Neural era: got right that representations should be learned, not designed — distributed embeddings through end-to-end transformers; its own inheritance-in-progress is transfer learning: pretrain once, adapt everywhere.

The synthesis an architect should say: production systems in 2026 are all three eras stacked — rules at the precision/guardrail floor, statistical machinery in retrieval and evaluation, neural models in the quality core; era-purism in either direction (all-rules nostalgia or all-LLM maximalism) is how systems get either brittle or unaffordable.
This question is really "do you understand why the stack looks like it does" — answer with the stack, not the dates.
questions.badge: Evergreen (the history question, asked to test judgment rather than trivia)
questions.oneLiner: Rules left the precision floor every system still stands on, statistics left the measurement discipline and the retrieval machinery, neural left learned representations — and a serious 2026 system is all three stacked, which is why era-purism in either direction is a design smell.

questions.text: Close it out: you're interviewing for AI Architect. Make the case that classical NLP fluency is leverage, not legacy.
points: The economics argument: at production volume, the cost ladder (rules → sparse+linear → small transformer → LLM) decides margins — knowing when TF-IDF+LR or a distilled model delivers LLM-grade outcomes at a thousandth the cost (Q14, Q25, Q28, Q37) is a line-item skill; the cascade pattern that captures it is classical NLP judgment.

The substrate argument: the LLM stack runs on classical machinery — BM25 in every hybrid retriever (Q16/17), IR metrics gating every RAG deploy (Q18), MinHash dedup and annotation discipline in every data pipeline (Q24/35), tokenization consequences in every bill (Q2). You can't architect what you can't decompose.

The diagnosis argument: when the fancy system misbehaves, failures localize to classical layers — retrieval slices, tokenizer fragmentation, label noise, eval mismatch (Q17, Q21, Q23, Q39) — and the engineer who can slice, bootstrap, and read errors by hand fixes in days what prompt-tweaking never finds.

The posture to project: not nostalgia but portfolio management — every classical technique is a cost-quality-latency-auditability point, and the architect's job is composing points, LLMs included, against requirements; the drills above are that portfolio, memorized.

End on the asymmetry: LLM knowledge depreciates with every release; the substrate — retrieval, evaluation, data discipline, structured prediction — is what every release still runs on. That's the closing sentence of the interview.
